https://www.barrons.com/articles/ams-ceo-everke-envisions-a-vast-universe-of-sensors-1525451368 Ams CEO Everke Envisions a Vast Universe of Sensors By Updated May 4, 2018 12:29 p.m. ET Text Size Ams AG CEO Alexander Everke. By Tiernan Ray Updated May 4, 2018 12:29 p.m. ET
In the world of chip makers, where lots of promising firms compete to get a share from giant customers, Apple ( AAPL ) being the Holy Grail, Austrian chip maker Ams AG ( AMS ) believes it has a path to selling more than just one single part at a time, instead gobbling up more and more of the value of a device.
If you’ve used Apple's iPhone X , you may have experienced “ Face ID ,” the thing that recognizes you and unlocks the device. The camera on the front of the phone that makes it possible uses parts from a variety of companies, including Lumentum ( LITE ), which makes the VCSEL laser diodes. Ams supplies the “ optical path ,” a component that makes sure transmission of light from laser to detector stays within tight tolerances necessary to function properly.
Chief Executive Alexander Everke , who took over two years ago, has a master plan to move beyond just the critical path, perhaps selling more and more to Apple in future models of iPhone, perhaps selling all the parts in some models of phones from competitors.
Everke, 55, a veteran of NXP Semiconductors ( NXPI ), has refashioned the company, selling off divisions and undertaking a slew of M&A deals, to create a one-stop shop for sensors , the devices that are increasingly the eyes and ears and fingers of artificial intelligence in a connected world.
Everke was kind enough to take a few minutes to chat over coffee in midtown Manhattan on Wednesday, while visiting from the company’s headquarters in Premstaetten , an Austrian town about two hours from Vienna.
"Sensors is the fastest growing segment of semis,” he observes. By rejiggering Ams’s assets, “We have built a unique portfolio,” contends Everke. "There is not a single company with the portfolio of what we have."
That portfolio is focused on four kinds of sensors : optical sensors, of the kind that can be of use in Face ID; image sensors, for things such as self-driving cars; audio sensors, such as microphones; and environmental sensors, which detect position, temperature, moisture, etc.
Expanding the Buffet, Taking Market Share
Today, the company’s role in the iPhone is a niche role, but an important one, according to David Dai of Bernstein , who recently initiated coverage of Ams’s stock with an Outperform rating. Dai thinks Ams could be one of the biggest beneficiaries of “augmented reality,” of which Face ID is just one form.
Dai expects Ams will increasingly sell more and more parts of the technology, pushing aside Lumentum and others in the iPhone and in phones running Google ’s Android software.
Everke seems to think so too. Ams, he tells me, has deep knowledge not only of the individual element, the optical path, but also what Lumentum and other suppliers are providing, because Ams now has comparable parts. It also has system software to make possible the various functions of all these optical components. He expects the totality of components and software to lead to more and more wins among smartphone makers.
"You can not design 3-D sensing software without also making the hardware, and vice versa ,” says Everke, who has a masters in electrical engineering.
"By designing the complete system there is a very strong benefit.” That should be especially true among competitors to Apple who don’t have the iPhone giant’s software history.
Everke believes there are other benefits his firm can bring to the non-Apple hopefuls. For example, Apple has patented a key approach to 3-D sensing, called " structured light .”
Ams has its own patents on an approach that can achieve the same results as structured light, but without infringing Apple’s claims. “We can help our customers achieve structured light, but it is a different way to do it.” Again, Ams is the outsourced R&D, if you will, of smartphone companies.
A Universe of Intriguing Sensing
Beyond 3-D sensing, Everke sees far broader opportunity in just about every part of electronics.
Everke’s views on sensors are brimming with not just possibilities, but works in progress. Ams is working with Amazon.com ( AMZN ) on the “Amazon Go” experimental retail locations, where image sensors know what you’ve got in your cart, and who you are, to smooth checkout.
His company is working with car makers to refine lidar , the technology used to map the road, for self-driving cars. The same technology can be applied to factory-floor robots that only need to see a foot or two around them to move parts.
Everke produces a small white cube from his pocket. “This can be more accurate as a heart-rate monitor than the arm band you usually use,” he says, referring to home heart-rate kits with the velcro closure and pump. Putting a finger on the small optical strip on top of the cube measures blood flow. Everke demonstrates the app for me on his phone. The rich display shows the beep-beep ups and downs of the heart rate, just like on a piece of medical equipment, along with all the stats, and history, of heart monitoring.
Another application for sensors will be detecting the composition of physical objects, such as food. It could be used for detecting potential allergens in things you eat, or just to know the nutrition value of a fruit or vegetable. (Similar to a company I’ve profiled in this space in years past, Consumer Physics of Israel. Everke indicated he expects Ams’s parts can make much more sleek, compact detection devices possible than what Consumer Physics offers.)
When It All Comes Together
Even broader possibilities loom as multiple sensors get built into devices in pairs that interact.
In cars , for example, Ams has been signing up billion-dollar deals with Tier 1 auto-parts suppliers that will include pairs of sensors fashioned together.
One possible example is the integration of optical and image sensors in the driver-side electronics of a car, providing face recognition .
“Today, you have this little memory button for the seat adjustment, so you can change it depending on who's using the car. Imagine with this sensor, you wouldn't have to even do that. It would detect who’s sitting and automatically adjust the seat.” That could be especially useful, he says, as more and more cars become part of the sharing economy , where many don’t own a car but rather just use an available one as needed.
He sees other combinations in mobile , such as combining microphones with environment sensors. “With the constant reduction in size of smartphones, more and more of the sockets [little holes in the frame of the device] are being taken out of the device, to make it more streamlined.
"So, what if you take the microphone hole, and you put a temperature sensor in the same slot. You could do that if you combine microphone and temperature sensor in a single chip."
Another example is combining the microphone with an optical sensor . Microphones a mechanical membranes that move back and forth in response to pressure of air waves. That pressure sets off electrical responses that produce the digital sound wave.
What if, says Everke, instead of the pressure of the membrane of the microphone, you could optically measure the undulations of that membrane having the optical sensor built into the microphone cavity observe the membrane? The result would be more precise sound response, he says, and therefore much higher audio quality.
Rebuilding the Company
To put together all of this opportunity, Everke had to do a lot of refashioning. "We were in too many lines of business,” he says, “we wanted to re-focus the company on sensors.” He sold off a division working on “ near-field communications ,” the stuff that makes possible wireless transfer of data between smartphones, to STMicroelectronics (STM). He sold off a unit focusing solely on power semiconductors to Dialog Semiconductor ( DLG ).
He also went on an acquisition spree, buying seven companies in the last 15 months. They include the U.S.’s Princeton Optronics , and Singapore ’s Heptagon Advanced Micro-Optics , the largest deal, at $900 million.
From 2,500 employees two and a half years ago, before Everke took over, the company has swelled to 11,000 people . Much of that was to build up the company’s manufacturing team in Asia.
He is proud that Ams didn’t get rid of anyone during that time. Engineers within the company were assigned to new roles as Ams shifted its focus more and more to sensors.
Achieving Balance
The downside of that is that bulking up leaves you vulnerable when orders suddenly come up short. That’s exactly what happened to Ams last quarter. The smartphone market has been under pressure, and Ams a week ago Tuesday offered a disappointing forecast for this quarter.
Bernstein’s Dai tied that directly to weakness in the iPhone, whose sales, announced by Apple this past Tuesday, were less than the Street was expecting.
There is no way, Everke explains, to just increase and then decrease manufacturing. “We could have taken staff off, but then you don't have time to ramp for the third quarter,” he observes. “It would be wrong to make changes to a company just for a quarter, I don't want to endanger our ability.”
Instead, says Everke, the goal will be to achieve greater stability in coming years. A factory that sits partly idle because so much comes from Apple, can in subsequent periods be utilized more fully, more of the time, as the company wins more contracts, from more and more customers, across the many products and markets that will be transformed by sensors.
"It's a step-by-step process,” says Everke, “of becoming a more and more predictable company."
Ams stock today closed up 1.88 Swiss francs, 2%, at CHF 90.30. The stock is up 42.8% in the past 12 months, and roughly 147% since Everke took over in October of 2015.
